📈 What This System Does

This decision-support system applies a validated machine learning model to predict long-term care demand at census-tract level across all 1,526 Wisconsin census tracts in all 72 counties. It forecasts how demand will evolve year by year from 2025 through 2035 and models access gaps by facility type, Nursing Facility, Home Health Agency, and Adult Day Services.

Every tract receives a current demand score, a risk tier, and a year-by-year demand trajectory. Use the Neighborhood Maps tab for the interactive choropleth map, Year-by-Year Forecast to compare scenarios, Disparity Analytics to see how access gaps differ across population groups, and Early Warning to identify tracts heading toward crisis.

ⓘ Built on real federal data (Census ACS 2022, TIGER/Line, CMS Care Compare, CDC PLACES). Values for 2025 to 2035 are scenario projections, not measurements, see Model & Methods tab.

Risk Tier Distribution, Overall LTC (2025)
Tiers are fixed quartiles of the 2025 score distribution, so the baseline year is 25% per tier by construction. Holding thresholds fixed is what makes tier escalation across projection years interpretable. See the Early Warning tab.

Year-by-Year Forecast: Adjust the year slider or press Play. Baseline applies documented federal trends (CMS facility closure rates, PHI workforce projections, SSA demographic projections, BRFSS disability trends). Optimistic assumes supply improvements; Pessimistic assumes accelerated deterioration.

⚠ Scope of these forecasts: the Overall LTC Demand trajectory is produced directly by the stacked ensemble applied to trend-adjusted tract features. The three service-type trajectories (Nursing Facility, Home Health, Adult Day Services) are currently shown as proportional approximations scaled from the Overall trajectory, not independent model runs. Service-specific forecasting is a documented next step. Read the service-type curves as indicative of direction and relative magnitude only.

On scenario spread: the three scenarios diverge modestly because the dominant index component, population age structure, carrying 45% combined weight, follows the same SSA projection in all three. Scenarios vary supply, workforce and disability trends only. This is a deliberate conservatism: demographic momentum through 2035 is already largely determined.

Communities with both high demand scores and limited economic resources face compound vulnerability, they need care most and are least able to access or finance it.

Why These Disparities Matter

Income level shapes LTC access in three ways: affordability (can the household pay for private care?), geography (lower-income tracts are disproportionately rural, where supply is thinnest), and health status (poverty is correlated with earlier onset of disability and chronic conditions that drive LTC need). Rural communities face a structural double burden, higher elderly shares and fewer facilities per capita, making them simultaneously the communities with the greatest demand and the fewest options. High-disability tracts show elevated demand scores across all four service types because disability prevalence directly predicts LTC service utilization. The proposed national system surfaces these compound vulnerabilities at census-tract resolution, enabling targeted intervention where conventional county-level averages would show no emergency.

Reading the numbers. Every score in this system is the LDI-T, the Long-Term Care Demand Index at census-tract level, scaled 0 to 100. Higher values mean greater unmet-need pressure. The index blends population need (63% of total weight) with supply shortfall (37%). It is not an accessibility measure, not a utilisation rate, and not a count of people. Service-type variants (Nursing Facility, Home Health, Adult Day Services) reweight the same components against the barrier that dominates for each service. Risk tier is the same number grouped into fixed quartiles of the 2025 distribution.
📋 Data Provenance: This system runs on real federal data. Tract boundaries are U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line cartographic files (2022), retrieved via tigris. Demographic and socioeconomic features are American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates (2018 to 2022), retrieved via tidycensus::get_acs(). Nursing facility supply is drawn from CMS Care Compare provider records, and chronic disease prevalence from CDC PLACES tract-level estimates. All 1,526 Wisconsin census tracts carry observed values; no feature is simulated. Projections for 2025 to 2035 are scenario estimates, produced by applying documented federal trend assumptions (SSA demographic projections, CMS facility closure rates, PHI workforce projections, BRFSS disability trends) to observed 2022 baselines. They are model projections, not measurements. Note that CDC PLACES values are themselves small-area model-based estimates rather than direct measurements.

Interpreting model fit: the ensemble is trained to predict LDI-T from its own constituent features, so a high R² is expected and indicates the model has learned the index structure well enough to extrapolate it to trend-adjusted inputs. It is not evidence that LDI-T correctly measures real-world access. External validation against observed utilisation and unmet-need outcomes is a planned next phase and has not yet been performed.

Per-service forecasts: the stacked ensemble projects the overall LDI-T. Service-type trajectories (Nursing Facility, Home Health, Adult Day Services) are scaled from each tract's own modelled overall growth ratio rather than fitted independently, so they preserve service-specific levels and tract-level heterogeneity but share a common growth driver. Independent per-service model fitting is a planned enhancement.

Tract count: 1,526 Wisconsin census tracts across all 72 counties, after excluding water-only tracts (ALAND = 0). Tract polygons are actual U.S. Census Bureau TIGER/Line cartographic boundaries (2022 vintage), geometrically simplified for browser rendering; simplification generalises boundary vertices only and does not alter tract identity or any computed value. The proposed national system extends this methodology to all ~74,000 U.S. census tracts across all 50 states.
